description: Insurance adjusters read your posts after your child is hurt. What not to post, why private accounts don't protect you, and why not to delete anything.
shortAnswer: Adjusters and defense lawyers look at social media in injury cases. They are looking for anything they can use to pay less. Treat everything you post as if the insurance adjuster will read it, and do not delete anything without talking to your lawyer first.

sections.heading: What they look for
sections.shortAnswer: A smile, activity, words about the wreck, and anything that blames you. None of this has to be true to cause trouble. A single picture, taken out of context, can take a long time to explain.

sections.heading: “My account is private” does not protect you
sections.shortAnswer: Privacy settings keep strangers out. They do not keep a lawsuit out. If your child's case is filed, the other side can ask for your posts, your messages, and your photos through the discovery process.

sections.heading: Do not delete what is already there
sections.shortAnswer: Once a lawsuit is reasonably foreseeable, Georgia law can put a duty on a party to preserve evidence. Destroying evidence after that point is called spoliation, and a court can punish it.

sections.heading: Your teenager is the biggest risk
sections.shortAnswer: Sit down with your teenager and explain why this matters. Ask them to stop posting about the wreck, the injury, and what they are doing while they recover.

sections.heading: Fundraising pages and family updates
sections.shortAnswer: Stick to what the family needs and how people can help. Leave out how the wreck happened and who was at fault. What you write should match what the doctors are writing in the medical records.

sections.heading: The other side’s social media can help your child
sections.shortAnswer: Look at the other driver's public pages, and save screenshots with the date showing. Do not contact the other driver, comment on their posts, or send friend requests.

sections.heading: What I tell parents to do
sections.shortAnswer: Stop posting about the wreck, the injury, and your child's activities until the case is over. Do not delete anything without asking your lawyer first. Talk to your teenager today.

faq.q: Can the insurance company use a photo of my injured child smiling against us?
faq.a: You were glad to see her happy for one afternoon. The insurance company sees a child who is “doing fine.” It will not see the night she cried from the pain, because you did not post that.

faq.q: Does a private social media account protect my posts in my child's injury case?
faq.a: Privacy settings keep strangers out. They do not keep a lawsuit out. A court can order them produced if they bear on the case. A friend can screenshot a post and pass it along.

faq.q: Should I delete my old posts after my child is hurt in Georgia?
faq.a: Do not do that without talking to your lawyer first. A jury may be told to assume that what you deleted would have hurt your case. A deleted photo of a smiling child can do far more damage than the photo itself ever would have.

faq.q: Can we still have a fundraising page for our injured child?
faq.a: That help can mean the world to a family. You do not have to give it up. Stick to what the family needs and how people can help. Leave out how the wreck happened and who was at fault.
